processing: Made mainly as a green tea with plump, downy leaf; a black tea version is also sold under the same appellation, tight and reddish with visible hairs.
harvest_season: Not given precisely; spring is the usual prized picking for a downy green tea of this kind.
appearance_dry: Plump buds of a fresh green, thickly covered in down.
appearance_liquor: Clear and transparent, a pale green-yellow.
appearance_wet: As is usual for a plump downy green, fat soft buds and young leaves.
taste_profile: Sweet and mellow with an orchid fragrance, fresh on the palate and able to take a few steeps.

brewing.notes: Use 85 to 90 C water at about 1 g to 50 ml. Pour in a little water to wet the leaf, add the tea, then fill; two or three steeps is about right.

vintage_note: As is usual for green tea, the green version is bought as the current year's harvest and best drunk within the year. Check whether the pack is green or black, because both carry the name, and look for the national geographical indication mark.
description:
Renhua Baimao is a white-haired tea from Renhua county in Shaoguan, northern Guangdong, the county that also holds the Danxia Mountain landscape. It has national geographical indication status, and the production centres on Hongshan, with Chengkou, Danxia, Dongtang, Wenshao and Huangkeng also in the zone.

Hongshan is high, cool and heavily forested, with an average altitude above 500 metres. The green version shows plump buds, thick down and a fresh colour; the black version is a tighter, reddish leaf with a floral lift.

The four things people repeat about it are fat buds, a full coat of hair, a sweet mellow taste and an orchid scent. Brew it at 85 to 90 C and stop after two or three steeps, as it gives its best early.

Most of it sells in Shaoguan and around Guangdong. Since the name covers both colours of tea, read the pack carefully and ask for the current year.
history:
The old name was Baimao, written 白茅. Local accounts put its creation in the Ming dynasty and call it a tribute tea by the Jiaqing reign of the Qing; these claims come from promotional sources, so treat them with care. Tea growing in Shaozhou, which included Qujiang and Renhua, is said to reach back to the Tang and Five Dynasties.

Its modern reputation rests on contests. It was named a Guangdong famous tea in 1992 and 1996, won a gold medal at a national forestry products fair in 1994, and took a first prize in the Zhongcha Cup in 2011.
